def: A long-acting form of erythropoietin that stimulates red cell production. Used for anemia of chronic kidney disease and chemotherapy; raises risk of thromboembolism.
A non-nucleoside inhibitor of the hepatitis C virus NS5B RNA polymerase, used in combination regimens.
Surgical removal of as much of a tumor as possible when it cannot be fully cured by surgery, as in advanced ovarian cancer, to make chemotherapy more effective.
A long-chain fatty acid ester attached to a drug, such as haloperidol or fluphenazine, so that an injection releases slowly over weeks in depot injections.
A GnRH receptor antagonist used for advanced prostate cancer. Lowers testosterone quickly without the initial flare seen with GnRH agonists.
An ultra-long-acting basal insulin analog lasting more than 24 hours.
A cholesterol precursor in skin that sunlight (UVB) converts to previtamin D3, which becomes cholecalciferol (vitamin D3).
Release of neutrophils stuck to blood vessel walls back into the circulating pool, raising the white cell count. Caused by glucocorticoids, epinephrine and stress.
Spontaneous loss of purine bases (adenine or guanine) from DNA, creating apurinic sites that are removed by base excision repair.
Collapse of previously open lung units, such as alveoli, which reduces the surface available for gas exchange. Seen in surfactant deficiency of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.
A skin condition in which light stroking produces raised red welts (wheals) within minutes, due to mast cell histamine release.
A handheld magnifying device with light used to inspect skin lesions in detail, especially to evaluate pigmented lesions for melanoma.
Shedding or peeling of the outer layer of skin, as in scarlet fever, Kawasaki disease and toxic shock syndrome.
Return of an erect penis to its flaccid state, mediated by sympathetic norepinephrine and the breakdown of cGMP.
Presence of dicarboxylic acids in urine from impaired fatty acid beta-oxidation, as in MCAD deficiency with hypoketotic hypoglycemia.
An oxidized form of the cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin, which is needed by phenylalanine hydroxylase. Defects in its recycling cause a form of phenylketonuria.
An intermediate in folate metabolism that dihydrofolate reductase converts to tetrahydrofolate. Methotrexate and trimethoprim block this enzyme.
A modified base found in the D-arm of tRNA, needed for the tRNA's folding.
A luminal amebicide used to clear Entamoeba histolytica cysts from the gut after tissue-invasive treatment with metronidazole.
The unit of lens refractive power (1 divided by focal length in meters). High myopia is greater than -6 diopters.
A chemical in the core of bacterial endospores that binds calcium and gives heat resistance.
Cocci that occur in pairs, such as Streptococcus pneumoniae (lancet-shaped), Neisseria (kidney-bean-shaped) and Moraxella.
Surgical removal of a diverticulum, an outpouching of a hollow organ, such as a Zenker diverticulum.
Surgery that suspends a diverticulum upward and fixes it in place instead of removing it, used for Zenker diverticulum.
Cutting through the wall of a diverticulum, here the common wall between a Zenker diverticulum and the esophagus, to drain it.
Bending the foot or hand upward, toward the shin or back of the forearm. Foot drop occurs with loss of ankle dorsiflexion.
A monoclonal antibody against PD-L1, a checkpoint inhibitor used for lung and bladder cancers.
Cells that lack adhesion to one another, as in lobular carcinoma from loss of E-cadherin, so cells infiltrate in single files.
Production of abnormal fibrinogen that does not work properly, causing a bleeding or clotting tendency with prolonged thrombin time.
Loss of coordinated muscle action, as in detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia where the bladder contracts while the sphincter fails to relax.
Polished, ivory-like exposed bone at a joint surface after cartilage is worn away, seen in osteoarthritis.
A kallikrein inhibitor that treats acute hereditary angioedema attacks by reducing bradykinin production.
A red blood cell with evenly spaced, short blunt projections (burr cell), seen in uremia and pyruvate kinase deficiency.
Appearing dark (hypoechoic) on ultrasound because the structure transmits sound waves with little echo, typical of fluid such as a cyst or abscess.
Involuntary imitation of another person's movements, seen in catatonia, schizophrenia and Tourette syndrome.
The pattern of echoes within a tissue on ultrasound. Altered echotexture in the testis may indicate torsion or tumor.
The outer part of the cervix that projects into the vagina, covered by squamous epithelium and meeting the endocervix at the transformation zone.
